maths_errors.text: Simple interest adds the same fixed amount each time; compound always gives a higher result.
maths_errors.correction: Compound interest is not always higher. Over one period, simple and compound interest give the same total (for example, £2,000 at 4% for 1 year gives £2,080 either way). Compound interest only gives the higher total when there are 2 or more periods and the rate is positive.

maths_errors.text: Compound interest gives a larger total because each period's interest is added to the running total before the next calculation.
maths_errors.correction: This is true only for 2 or more periods with a positive rate. For a single period the two totals are equal.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: define percentage as ‘number of parts per hundred’
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson never says what a percentage is. It starts straight from percentage change.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: interpret percentages and percentage changes as a fraction or a decimal, and interpret these multiplicatively
missing_spec_content.why: Decimal multipliers appear (1.20, 0.80), but the lesson never explains why 20% equals 0.20 or 1/5. Fraction equivalents are never shown.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: express one quantity as a percentage of another
missing_spec_content.why: Only percentage change is taught. Writing one quantity as a percentage of another (for example, 30 out of 120 as a percentage) is never taught.
The concept slide mentions comparing changes fairly, but no method or example of comparing two quantities using percentages is given.
Percentages above 100% (for example, a 150% increase giving multiplier 2.5, or 'new value is 120% of old') are never mentioned.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: simple interest including in financial mathematics
missing_spec_content.why: Simple interest appears only as the formula 'I = PRT/100' in keyFacts. The letters P, R and T are never defined, and no method is taught.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: set up, solve and interpret the answers in growth and decay problems, including compound interest
missing_spec_content.why: A = P × mⁿ is stated, but setting up a growth or decay problem and interpreting the answer is not taught. Examples of what is missing: depreciation, population growth, or working out how many years until a value passes a target.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: and work with general iterative processes
missing_spec_content.why: Iterative processes (repeatedly applying a rule, such as u(n+1) = 1.05u(n) − 20) are not mentioned at all.

density.text: % change = (change ÷ original) × 100 | Increase multiplier = 1 + (r/100) | Decrease multiplier = 1 − (r/100) | Compound: A = P × mⁿ
density.why: Four separate formulas are packed into one line with pipe separators. A first-time learner cannot take these in at once.

density.text: To find percentage change: subtract original from new to get the change, divide by the original, then multiply by 100. If positive it is an increase; if negative it is a decrease. For applying a % increase or decrease: multiply by 1 + r/100 (increase) or 1 − r/100 (decrease), where r is the percentage. For compound interest or depreciation: A = P × mⁿ, where P is the starting amount, m is the multiplier, and n is the number of periods. For reverse percentage (finding the original): divide the known value by the multiplier.
density.why: One paragraph explains four different methods. Reverse percentage is introduced here without any formula on the slide.

This contradicts the formula slide ('subtract original from new') and keyFacts[0] ('Change = new − original'). Those give −40, which signals a decrease. The switch of sign convention is not explained.

density.text: Check using the multiplier: a 25% decrease means multiplying by 0.75. £160 × 0.75 = £120 ✓.
density.why: The instruction already contains the full working. It also uses the multiplier idea without saying why 25% off gives 0.75.

density.text: Compound interest applies the multiplier repeatedly — each year's interest is calculated on the new total, not just the original, so the amount grows faster than simple interest.
density.why: One sentence carries three ideas: repeated multiplier, interest on the new total, and comparison with simple interest. Simple interest has not been defined at this point.

density.text: Adding the same percentage back undoes a percentage of the wrong base.
density.why: The phrase is too compressed to follow. It needs to say that 30% of £350 is smaller than 30% of the original £500, so adding it back falls short.

density.text: calculating 4% × 3 = 12% total, giving £2,240 instead of applying the multiplier 1.04 three times to get £2,249.73.
density.why: Both methods are compressed into one line with no intermediate values. The compound working (2000 × 1.04³ = 2000 × 1.124864) is not shown.

density.text: Simple interest gives the same fixed amount each period (I = PRT/100).
density.why: P, R and T are never defined anywhere in the lesson.

density.text: do not round intermediate answers or compound errors build up
density.why: 'Compound' here means 'add up', not compound interest. This ambiguous wording could confuse the learner in a compound interest lesson.
